Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding focus · Whole-school assembly

Calling for help

What to say, who to tell, and how to get help safely.

20 minutes
Think, point, speak or watch.
Nobody is put on the spot.

When you dial 999, what is the very first question the operator asks?

Discussion / choices: Which service do you need? · Why did you not fix it yourself? · What is your postcode from memory?

Key idea: The operator asks 'Which service do you need?' (Ambulance, Police, or Fire) and then guides you calmly step by step.

Presenter: Introduce the focus calmly: knowing what to say and who to tell so nobody freezes or feels scared to ask for help.

02 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

One call changes everything

1.5–4 min

Watch the scene. Pause at the prediction point and name what the caller should tell the operator.

You do not need medical training to save a life — making the call starts the help.

MADE BY MATT · ORIGINAL ANIMATIONOFFLINE

Someone collapses on the ground and will not wake up. A bystander takes a slow breath and checks it is safe to approach. Pause here: the operator answers 'Emergency, which service?' What are the four key things the caller needs to do? The caller asks for an ambulance, gives the road and landmark, describes what happened clearly, and stays on the phone. One calm call brings trained paramedics to the exact spot. You never have to handle an emergency alone.

PAUSE · PREDICT · REPLAY

Prediction point — what four pieces of information help emergency services reach you fast?

Captioned · works offline without internet · optional local video slot

Scene summary / still alternative
  1. Spotting that someone needs urgent help: Someone collapses on the ground and will not wake up. A bystander takes a slow breath and checks it is safe to approach.
  2. Dialling 999 calmly: Pause here: the operator answers 'Emergency, which service?' What are the four key things the caller needs to do?
  3. Service · Where · What happened · Stay on the line: The caller asks for an ambulance, gives the road and landmark, describes what happened clearly, and stays on the phone.
  4. Help arrives: One calm call brings trained paramedics to the exact spot. You never have to handle an emergency alone.

Discussion / choices: Watch the scene. Pause at the prediction point and name what the caller should tell the operator.

Key idea: Every 999 call uses four steps: 1. Which service · 2. Where you are · 3. What is happening · 4. Stay on the line.

Presenter: Play the built-in offline animation and pause at the prediction point. Reassure pupils that the operator asks the questions one by one.

03 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

The four steps of a 999 call

4–6 min

Tap the four parts of an emergency call in the order they happen.

If you do not know the postcode, name the road, school, shop, or landmark nearby.

Discussion / choices: STAY ON THE LINE · WHERE ARE YOU? · WHICH SERVICE? · WHAT IS HAPPENING?

Key idea: WHICH SERVICE? → WHERE ARE YOU? → WHAT IS HAPPENING? → STAY ON THE LINE.

Presenter: Remind pupils never to hang up until the operator says it is okay, because the operator will talk them through what to do next.

04 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

Practise the call: urgent emergencies

6–8.5 min

Choose the safest action for each emergency situation.

Keeping yourself safe comes first so you can make the call.

Discussion / choices: Choose the safest action for each emergency situation.

Key idea: In any emergency: get yourself safe first, ask for the right service on 999, give the location, and follow the operator's instructions.

Presenter: Emphasise personal safety in street or fire scenarios: never jump into a fight or go back inside a burning building.

05 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

When you feel unsafe at home, outside, or inside yourself

8.5–11 min

Tap each situation to see what you are allowed to do to stay safe.

No one is ever allowed to hurt you, and you never have to carry danger alone.

If anyone is in danger right now, you are allowed to call 999 — even about your own family. It is never your fault. You can also tell your Safeguarding Lead at school or call Childline on 0800 1111.
Head straight to a bright, busy place or into a shop and tell staff, rather than taking a quiet shortcut alone. Call 999 if you are in danger.
Tell a trusted adult straight away, call Childline free on 0800 1111, or text SHOUT to 85258 if texting feels easier than speaking.

Discussion / choices: Someone at home is hurting me or someone else · I think I am being followed or feel unsafe walking · I feel overwhelmed or unsafe in myself

Key idea: Whether the danger is outside, at home, or how you are feeling inside, reaching out for help is always allowed and never your fault.

Presenter: Read these responses calmly and matter-of-factly. Remind pupils that asking for help is a strength.

06 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

When it is not safe to speak out loud

11–13 min

On a mobile phone, what can you do if you dial 999 but cannot speak safely?

The police Silent Solution system is built for moments when speaking out loud puts you at risk.

Discussion / choices: 1. Still dial 999 · 2. Listen to the operator · 3. Press 55 when asked

Key idea: Dial 999, stay on the line, and press 55 when prompted on a mobile if you cannot speak safely.

Presenter: Explain clearly that pressing 55 works after dialling 999 on a mobile when prompted by the system.

07 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

Which number or person fits the need?

13–15 min

Tap each contact route to see when to use it.

Not every worry needs an ambulance or police car — there is a right door for every need.

Use 999 when life or safety is in danger right now. Use 101 for non-urgent police reports, and 111 for medical advice when it is not life-threatening.
Childline (0800 1111) and Shout (text 85258) are free, private, and open day or night for any worry when you want someone to listen.
Teachers, support staff, and the Safeguarding Lead in school are there to listen, help keep you safe, and get the right support.

Discussion / choices: 999 (Urgent emergency) · 101 (Police non-urgent) · 111 (NHS advice) · 0800 1111 (Childline) · Text SHOUT to 85258 · A trusted adult or Safeguarding Lead in school

Key idea: 999 is for danger right now; 101 and 111 are for non-urgent help; 0800 1111, text 85258, and trusted adults in school are there for any worry.

Presenter: Point out where helpline numbers are displayed around school so pupils do not have to memorise them.

08 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

Will I get in trouble for calling?

15–17 min

This worry stops people asking for help. Tap the three highlighted truths.

Let's settle the biggest worry clearly.

You for asking for help in good faith, being hurt is , and telling a is how things get safer.

NO TROUBLE: If you are genuinely worried someone is hurt or unsafe, you will never be punished for calling.

NOT YOUR FAULT: If someone is hurting or threatening you, the blame belongs to them, never to you.

SAFE ACTION: Keeping danger a secret protects the problem; telling a trusted adult protects people.

Discussion / choices: never get in trouble · never your fault · trusted adult

Key idea: You never get in trouble for getting help in good faith, and being hurt is never your fault.

Presenter: Reinforce this message calmly: genuine calls for help are always supported.

09 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

Ways to ask for help in school

17–18.5 min

What if saying the words out loud feels too difficult?

You do not need perfect words to start the conversation.

Discussion / choices: Use one short starter sentence · Write a note or point to a card · Bring a friend or support worker

Key idea: Whether you speak, write a note, point to a card, or bring someone with you, staff will listen and help.

Presenter: Remind pupils who the safeguarding team are in school and where they can be found.

10 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 1 · Safeguarding · Getting help

Ready to get help safely

18.5–20 min

Choose the two true reminders from today's assembly.

Think, point, or keep your answer private.

Discussion / choices: On 999: state the service, where you are, what is happening, and stay on the line · Keep danger a secret in case someone gets annoyed · You never get in trouble for asking for help or telling a trusted adult

Key idea: Know the four 999 call steps, use 999 press 55 if you cannot speak, and remember you are always allowed to ask a trusted adult for help.

Presenter: End calmly. Ensure staff are available at the doors if any pupil wishes to speak privately.

Word help

emergency
When someone's life is in danger, someone is seriously hurt, or a crime or fire is happening right now.
operator
The trained call handler who answers 999, 101, or 111 and guides you step by step.
silent solution
Calling 999 on a mobile phone and pressing 55 when prompted if it is not safe to speak out loud.
trusted adult
A teacher, safeguarding lead, support worker, or family member who helps keep you safe.
confidential
Kept private by a helpline or service unless someone is in danger and needs protection.

Teacher desk

20-minute assembly · secondary SEMH

Participation and delivery

Read every prompt and option aloud. Pupils may answer by pointing, thumbs, speaking, or simply watching. Staff operate the board; nobody needs to type. Allow processing time. Do not require eye contact or invite personal disclosures.

High-sensitivity topic covering emergencies, feeling unsafe in the street or at home, and how to contact 999, 101, 111, Childline (0800 1111), Shout (85258), or a trusted adult in school. Keep the tone calm and factual. Watch for anyone who appears quiet or distressed, and pass any disclosure to the Safeguarding Lead the same day.
